verses.context: The first birth in the Bible follows directly on the expulsion from Eden. Eve names her son and speaks the first words recorded of her outside the garden, a cry that credits the LORD with the child. The hope of 3:15 and 3:20 now has a face.
verses.grammar: "Had relations with" is yada, the ordinary verb ‘to know’, used here and often in Genesis for sexual union; it frames the act as personal knowledge, not merely physical. Eve's words are compressed: qaniti ish et-YHWH, ‘I have acquired a man with the LORD’. Qaniti sounds like Qayin (Cain). The small word et is the problem. Most take it as the preposition ‘with’, meaning ‘with the LORD's help’, as the BSB reads. It is also the form of the Hebrew object marker, and Martin Luther's translation read ‘I have gotten the man, the LORD’, as if Eve thought her son was the promised deliverer. Most modern grammarians find the prepositional reading more natural. Calling a newborn an ish, ‘a man’, is unusual and may reflect pride, or the sense that a new adult human life has begun.

theology.note: Eve attributes the gift of life to the LORD even after the sentence of 3:16. Childbirth is painful, but it is still God's work, and Scripture continues to treat children as his gift (Psalm 127:3).

verses.context: A second son, Abel, is born without any naming speech. The verse then introduces the brothers by their work: Abel keeps sheep, Cain works the ground. The narrator names Abel's work first, though Cain is the elder.
verses.grammar: Vattosef laledet, ‘she added to bear’, is the usual Hebrew way to say ‘again’ or ‘later’. Abel's name, hevel, is the word for breath or vapor. The two occupations are participles describing ongoing identity: ro'eh tson, ‘a shepherd of flock’, and oved adamah, ‘a worker of the ground’. Oved is the verb of 2:5, 2:15, and 3:23, so Cain carries on the task given to Adam.
verses.history: Farming and herding were the two basic economies of the ancient Near East, and they were interdependent: villages grew grain and kept flocks, and herders moved flocks through farmland in season. Genesis does not rank the two. Abel's brief life will be remembered, not his occupation.

verses.context: The first act of worship in the Bible. Cain brings some produce, and Abel brings from the firstborn of his flock and their fat. The description is careful: Abel's gift is qualified as first and best, Cain's is not qualified at all.
verses.grammar: "In the course of time" is miqqets yamim, ‘at the end of days’, perhaps a season's end or harvest. Both gifts are called minchah, "offering", a word that means a gift or tribute (a subject's payment to a king in Judges 3:15) and later names the grain offering in Leviticus 2. Abel "also" brought (hevi gam hu, ‘he too brought’), and his gift is "the firstborn" (bekhorot) and chelvehen, literally ‘their fat portions’, which the BSB renders "the best portions". The fat was the part later reserved for the LORD in Israel's sacrifices (Leviticus 3:16).

theology.note: Hebrews 11:4 says that by faith Abel offered a better sacrifice. The verse itself shows the outward difference, first and best against some; Hebrews locates the inward one, a heart that trusted God. The quality of the gift expresses the worshiper, which is why the text speaks of God regarding Abel and his offering, the person first.

verses.context: Having regarded Abel and his offering (verse 4), the LORD does not regard Cain and his. The text does not say how the difference was shown, and it gives no explicit reason. Cain's response, burning anger and a fallen face, becomes the focus.
verses.grammar: Sha'ah ("looked with favor") is a verb of looking with attention; it is used in both clauses, positively and negatively. The order matters: God regards ‘Abel and his offering’, then not ‘Cain and his offering’, the person before the gift. "Cain became very angry" is literally ‘it burned to Cain exceedingly’ (vayyichar), the Hebrew idiom for anger as heat. "His countenance fell" (vayyippelu panav) pictures a face cast down in resentment or dejection, the posture God addresses in verses 6 and 7.

theology.note: The story withholds the reason for God's choice and puts the spotlight on Cain's reaction. That reaction, anger at God and envy of a brother, is what the rest of the chapter traces. 1 John 3:12 says Cain's own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.

verses.context: Before any crime, God speaks to Cain, asks why he is angry, and warns him. The warning offers a choice: do well and be accepted, or face a sin already crouching at the door. It is the first time the word sin appears in the Bible.
verses.grammar: Verse 7 is among the hardest sentences in Genesis. Se'et ("accepted") is literally ‘a lifting up’; it can mean acceptance, forgiveness (the lifting of guilt), or the lifting of Cain's fallen face. "Crouching" (rovets) is a masculine participle, while chattat, ‘sin’, is feminine; the mismatch has led some scholars to connect robets with an Akkadian word for a demon that lurks at doorways, and others to read ‘sin is a croucher’. The last clause repeats 3:16 almost word for word: teshuqato ("it desires you") and timshol ("you must master it"). The imperfect timshol can be read as command (‘you must rule’), promise (‘you will rule’), or even question (‘will you rule?’); most translations take it as a command.

theology.note: Sin is pictured as an active power seeking to master a person, yet Cain is not helpless before it. The verse holds together what the rest of Scripture keeps: sin's real force and human responsibility to resist it (Romans 6:12-14, James 1:14-15).
God warns before he judges. The questions are an invitation to turn back while the choice is still open, the same pattern the prophets follow when they call Israel to do well before judgment falls.

verses.context: Cain speaks to Abel, and when they are in the field he rises up and kills him. The first death in the Bible is not old age but murder, and it comes one generation after the fall. The word ‘brother’ runs through the passage (seven times from verse 2 to verse 11), pressing the horror of the act.
verses.grammar: "Rose up against" (vayyaqom el) describes an attack, as in Deuteronomy 22:26 of a man attacking his neighbor. "Killed" is harag, the ordinary verb for violent killing, used again by Lamech in verse 23. The narration is bare: no dialogue in the field, no description of the act, only the two verbs.
verses.text: The standard Hebrew text says ‘Cain said to his brother Abel’ and then reports no words, as if something has dropped out. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Latin Vulgate supply "Let us go out to the field", and the BSB follows them. Other translations keep the Hebrew and render ‘Cain spoke to Abel’ or ‘told Abel’.

theology.note: The first murder is the killing of a brother. Scripture treats every murder in that light: 9:6 grounds the prohibition of murder in the image of God, and Jesus traces murder back to anger and contempt toward a brother (Matthew 5:21-22).

verses.context: God's question echoes 3:9. He asked Adam ‘Where are you?’ and now asks Cain where his brother is. Cain answers with a lie and a sneering counter-question.
verses.grammar: "I do not know" (lo yadati) is a flat lie, a step beyond Adam's excuses. "Am I my brother's keeper?" is a question with the interrogative he attached to shomer, a participle of shamar, the verb for guarding and keeping that described Adam's charge in 2:15 and the cherubim's watch in 3:24. The implied answer Cain expects is no; the whole Bible answers yes.

theology.note: Cain's question denies responsibility for his brother. Scripture's answer runs from the law's command to love the neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) to John's teaching that anyone who hates his brother is a murderer, while love lays down its life for the brothers (1 John 3:15-16).

verses.context: God's second question, "What have you done?", echoes his words to Eve in 3:13. Then he tells Cain what he knows: Abel's blood cries out from the ground. No human witness saw the murder, but God heard.
verses.grammar: "Blood" is plural, demei, ‘bloods’, the form Hebrew often uses for blood that has been shed violently. Later Jewish teaching in the Mishnah drew from the plural that Cain had killed Abel and all the descendants who would have come from him. "Cries out" is tso'aqim, the verb for the outcry of the wronged and oppressed calling for help, the cry God promises to hear from the widow and orphan in Exodus 22:22-23.

theology.note: Innocent blood has a voice before God even when no human court hears it. Scripture repeats the theme in the souls under the altar crying for justice (Revelation 6:9-10), and Hebrews sets Christ's blood beside Abel's as speaking a better word (Hebrews 12:24).

The verb for Abel's blood crying out is the same verb Scripture uses for the cry of the powerless whom God hears. The first victim of violence becomes the first voice God attends to on behalf of someone who could not defend himself.

verses.context: Cain is cursed, the first human being in the Bible to be cursed directly (in chapter 3 the curse fell on the serpent and the ground). The ground that drank his brother's blood will now refuse him its strength, and the farmer becomes a restless wanderer.
verses.grammar: "Cursed and banished from the ground" renders arur attah min ha'adamah. The preposition min can mean ‘from’ in the sense of separation (driven away from the ground) or source (cursed by the ground that witnessed the crime); the BSB combines both ideas. The ground "opened its mouth" (patsetah et-piha), the phrase used when the earth swallows Korah's company (Numbers 16:30). In verse 12, "a fugitive and a wanderer" is a rhyming pair in Hebrew, na vanad, ‘a staggering one and a drifting one’.

theology.note: The punishment fits the crime: the man who poured blood into the ground loses the ground's yield. Scripture repeatedly pictures bloodshed as polluting the land (Numbers 35:33), so that violence against people is also a wound to creation.

verses.context: Cain protests. He complains of the weight of his sentence and lists its parts: driven from the ground, hidden from God's face, a wanderer, and exposed to anyone who would kill him. He says nothing of Abel.
verses.grammar: Avoni ("my punishment") is from avon, a word that means both iniquity and the punishment it brings. Minnesso, ‘for bearing’, uses nasa, to carry or to lift away; ‘bearing iniquity’ elsewhere can mean forgiving it (Exodus 34:7). So the sentence can mean ‘my punishment is too heavy to bear’ or ‘my iniquity is too great to be forgiven’. "You have driven me" (gerashta) is the verb of 3:24, where the LORD drove out the man. "I will be hidden" is a Niphal of satar: being hidden from God's face is the opposite of the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25).
verses.text: English Bibles divide over verse 13. Most modern versions read ‘My punishment is greater than I can bear’, while some older and marginal renderings read ‘My iniquity is greater than can be forgiven’. The Hebrew allows both, because avon and nasa each carry both senses.

verses.context: God answers Cain's fear with protection: anyone who kills him will face sevenfold vengeance, and God sets a sign on him. Cain leaves the LORD's presence and settles in Nod, east of Eden, the direction of exile.
verses.grammar: "Will be avenged" (yuqqam) is a Hophal, a passive form of naqam, to avenge. God does not authorize anyone to avenge Abel; he claims vengeance himself. "Placed a mark on Cain" is literally ‘set a sign for Cain’, ot, which can be read as a mark on his body or a sign given to him. Nod means ‘wandering’ and is formed from the same root as nad in verse 12: the wanderer lives in the Land of Wandering.
verses.text: The standard Hebrew text begins God's reply with lakhen, ‘therefore’. The Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate read lo ken, ‘not so’, which differs by one letter, and the BSB follows them with "Not so". Translations that keep the Hebrew read ‘Therefore, whoever kills Cain...’ or ‘Very well’.

theology.note: God reserves vengeance to himself (Deuteronomy 32:35) and restrains the spiral of blood feud. The guilty man is judged, yet his life is protected, a mercy the chapter's next murderer, Lamech, will twist into a boast.

Cain goes out "from the presence of the LORD", further east than his parents. Genesis keeps tracking eastward movement away from God (11:2), and the reversal of that exile is one of Scripture's great hopes.

verses.context: Cain has a son, Enoch, and builds a city. The wanderer sentenced to restlessness founds the first settled place in the Bible, and names it for his son.
verses.grammar: "Built a city" is literally ‘was building a city’ (vayhi boneh ir), a participle describing ongoing activity. The subject of the participle is naturally Cain, but grammatically it could be Enoch, the last-named man; some scholars propose that Enoch built the city and named it after his own son Irad, noting the likeness of Irad to Eridu, the city Mesopotamian tradition counted as the first. Most translations take Cain as the builder. Ir ("city") can mean any walled settlement, however small.

theology.note: City building begins in the line of Cain, but Scripture does not condemn the city as such; it ends with the city of God (Revelation 21:2). Human culture can be a way of securing oneself apart from God, as at Babel (11:4), or can be gathered into God's purposes.

verses.context: A short genealogy carries Cain's line to Lamech, the seventh generation from Adam through Cain. Several names resemble those in Seth's line in chapter 5 (Enoch, Irad and Jared, Mehujael and Mahalalel, Methushael and Methuselah, Lamech).
verses.grammar: The first clause is passive, vayyivaled, ‘and there was born to Enoch’ (a Niphal), and then the list switches to the active yalad, ‘fathered’. This brief ‘A fathered B’ pattern is the simplest form of biblical genealogy, a single line with no ages, unlike the fuller pattern of chapter 5.
verses.history: Interpreters explain the similarity between Cain's line and Seth's in two main ways. Many critical scholars think two versions of one ancient list have been preserved. Others see a deliberate contrast: two lines with similar names, one ending in Lamech's boast of vengeance, the other in a Lamech who hopes for comfort (5:29) and an Enoch who walks with God (5:24).

verses.context: Lamech takes two wives, the first case of polygamy in the Bible. The narrator makes no comment, but the pattern of 2:24, one man joined to his wife, has already been set.
verses.grammar: "Married" is vayyiqqach lo, ‘took for himself’, the ordinary expression for taking a wife. The names Adah and Zillah are usually connected with ‘ornament’ and ‘shade’, though meanings of names in these early chapters are uncertain.

theology.note: Genesis records polygamy without endorsing it, and its stories of households with more than one wife (Abraham, Jacob, Elkanah) are full of rivalry and grief. Jesus returns to the one-flesh pattern of 2:24 as God's design from the beginning (Matthew 19:4-6).

verses.context: Lamech's children found three ways of life: herding in tents, music, and metalwork. A daughter, Naamah, is also named, rare in a genealogy. The line of a murderer produces the arts and crafts on which every later culture depends.
verses.grammar: Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-cain have similar sounding names, as if built on a common root associated with bringing or carrying. "Father" (av) here means founder or originator of a way of life, as in "the father of all who play the harp and flute". Kinnor is a lyre, the instrument David played for Saul (1 Samuel 16:23); ugav is probably a pipe or flute. Tubal-cain is "a forger" (lotesh, a sharpener or hammerer) of tools in nechoshet ("bronze", or copper) and barzel ("iron").
verses.history: Lyres are among the oldest well-documented instruments of the region; richly decorated examples were found in the Royal Cemetery at Ur in southern Iraq, from around the middle of the third millennium BC. Tent-dwelling pastoralists living beside settled towns were a constant feature of the ancient Near East, as the stories of Abraham and his family show.

theology.note: Music, craft, and animal husbandry are presented as human achievements, not gifts stolen from the gods. Scripture elsewhere credits skill in craftsmanship to God's Spirit (Exodus 31:3-5), so the gifts are good even when their first bearers were far from him.

verses.context: Lamech's song, the first poem since the man's delight in 2:23, is a boast of killing. Where God had promised sevenfold vengeance to protect Cain, Lamech claims seventy-sevenfold for himself.
verses.grammar: The poem is built in parallel lines: "hear my voice" // ‘listen to my speech’; ‘a man’ // ‘a young man’; ‘wound’ // ‘bruise’. The two nouns for his injuries, petsa (‘wound’) and chabburah (‘bruise’ or ‘stripe’), are the same pair that appear in the law of proportionate justice, ‘wound for wound, stripe for stripe’ (Exodus 21:25). Lamech takes a life for a bruise, the opposite of proportion. "Have slain" is harag, Cain's verb in verse 8. The numbers climb from shiv'atayim, ‘sevenfold’, to shiv'im veshiv'ah, ‘seventy-seven’.

theology.note: Sin has grown from Cain's hidden murder, followed by fear, to open killing celebrated in verse. God's protection of Cain is turned into a license for unlimited revenge.

When Peter asks how often to forgive, Jesus answers with seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22), the number of Lamech's vengeance in the Greek of Genesis. Many readers see a deliberate reversal: limitless forgiveness in place of limitless revenge.

verses.context: The narrative returns to Adam and Eve. A third son is born, and Eve names him Seth, explaining that God has appointed another seed in place of Abel. The line of promise continues through him, as chapter 5 will show.
verses.grammar: Shet ("Seth") sounds like shat, "has granted" (literally ‘has appointed’ or ‘has set’), the verb Eve uses. The same verb, shit, was God's in 3:15: ‘I will put enmity’. Zera acher, "another seed", picks up the key word of 3:15, the woman's seed. Eve speaks of Elohim here, not the LORD as in verse 1.

theology.note: The murder of Abel does not end the promise of 3:15. God provides another seed, and the line through Seth becomes the line that leads to Noah, Abraham, and ultimately, in Luke's genealogy, to Jesus (Luke 3:38).

verses.context: Seth has a son, Enosh, and the chapter ends on a note of worship: people began to call on the name of the LORD. After the song of vengeance comes the first sign of a community turning to God.
verses.grammar: Enosh means ‘man’ or ‘humankind’, a word used in poetry for human beings in their frailty (Psalm 8:4, 103:15). "Men began" is huchal, a Hophal (passive) of the verb chalal, ‘it was begun’. "To call upon the name of the LORD" (liqro beshem YHWH) is the phrase used when Abram builds altars and worships (12:8, 13:4). It covers prayer, worship, and proclaiming God's name.
verses.text: Ancient versions read the clause differently. The Septuagint makes Enosh the subject, saying he hoped to call on the name of the LORD. Some Jewish tradition, reading chalal in its other sense, ‘to profane’, took the verse to mean that the name began to be profaned in idolatry. Most modern translations follow the plain sense of the standard Hebrew: people began to call on the LORD. Readers have also asked how this fits Exodus 6:3, where God says he was not known to the patriarchs by the name YHWH; common answers are that Exodus 6 speaks of knowing the name's meaning through the exodus, or that Genesis uses the familiar name for the God whom the early generations worshiped.

theology.note: The first mention of public prayer in Scripture stands at the end of a chapter of violence. Calling on the LORD's name is presented as the mark of the line that God preserves, the phrase Joel and Paul use of those who will be saved (Joel 2:32, Romans 10:13).
